claim: Pet1 neurons are generated from Pet1-positive postmitotic precursors located in the embryonic ventral hindbrain from the isthmus to the caudal region of the myelencephalon.
source: 5-HT neurons are generated from Pet1-positive postmitotic precursors located in the embryonic ventral hindbrain from the isthmus to the caudal region of the myelencephalon (Alonso et al., 2013; Hendricks et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Alonso et al., 2013; Hendricks et al., 1999).

claim: At E14.5, Pet1 neurons have 68,871 peaks of transposase accessible chromatin (TAC).
source: We generated ATAC-seq biological replicates with a mean of 29M unique paired-end mapped reads per sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d-g) and identified 68,871 peaks of transposase accessible chromatin (TAC) at E14.5
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental ATAC-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pet1-negative cells have 59,323 TACs at E14.5.
source: and 59,323 TACs in an equal number of control Yfp-negative, Pet1-negative cells ('Pet1neg') collected from the same hindbrain regions at the same developmental age, which comprise diverse non-serotonergic cell types.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental ATAC-seq data from control cells.

claim: Cell type identity accounted for 93% of the variance when comparing Pet1 neuron ATAC-seq replicates with Pet1neg ATAC-seq samples and with previously published ATAC-seq datasets.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that cell type identity accounted for 93% of the variance when comparing Pet1 neuron ATAC-seq replicates with Pet1neg ATAC-seq samples and with previously published ATAC-seq datasets obtained from bulk tissue dissections (Figure 1a; Gorkin et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1a and comparison with published datasets.

claim: 31% of TACs identified in Pet1 neurons at E14.5 are unique and not found in Pet1neg cells.
source: Indeed, of the TACs we identified in Pet1 neurons at E14.5, 31% are unique (Pet1 neuron-specific TACs) and not found in Pet1neg cells
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of ATAC-seq data between Pet1 neurons and Pet1neg cells.

claim: 22% of TACs in Pet1 neurons at E14.5 are not previously identified in any other cell type.
source: and 22% are not previously identified in any other cell type (Gorkin et al., 2020; Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previously published ENCODE datasets.

claim: Active and poised distal enhancer regions are over-represented among the Pet1 neuron-specific TACs.
source: Active and poised distal enhancer regions are over-represented among the Pet1 neuron-specific TACs (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChromHMM analysis of histone modifications shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ChIPmentation analysis identified 1919 genomic regions that fulfill the criteria for super-enhancers based on the presence of unusually expansive H3K27ac signals.
source: Our ChIPmentation analysis also identified 1919 genomic regions that fulfill the criteria for super-enhancers based on the presence of unusually expansive H3K27ac signals (Figure 1d; Lovén et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIPmentation data and analysis using established super-enhancer criteria from published methods.

claim: 42% of the super-enhancers detected in Pet1 neurons were not detected in bulk mouse forebrain, hindbrain, or liver tissues.
source: Comparing these to previously annotated enhancers in other cell types (Gorkin et al., 2020), we found that a significant percentage (42%) of the super-enhancers we detected in Pet1 neurons were not detected in bulk mouse forebrain, hindbrain, or liver tissues (Figure 1e)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previously published enhancer annotations.

claim: A 82.9 kb super-enhancer detected in Pet1 neurons but not Pet1neg neurons spans the Lmx1b locus.
source: As an example, a 82.9 kb super-enhancer detected in Pet1 neurons but not Pet1neg neurons spans the Lmx1b locus (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIPmentation data showing H3K27ac and H3K4me1 enrichment at the Lmx1b locus.

claim: A distinct TAC was found immediately upstream of the Pet1 promoter in Pet1 neurons but not in Pet1neg cells.
source: Notably, a distinct TAC was found immediately upstream of the Pet1 promoter in Pet1 neurons but not in Pet1neg cells (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The upstream region of Pet1 directs robust reporter expression to developing and adult 5-HT neurons present in each of the midbrain, pontine, and medullary raphe nuclei.
source: Previous transgenic assays, in vivo, demonstrated that this upstream region directs robust reporter expression to developing and adult 5-HT neurons present in each of the midbrain, pontine, and medullary raphe nuclei (Krueger and Deneris, 2008; Scott et al., 2005a; Scott et al., 2005b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous transgenic studies.

claim: 38% of all experimentally validated VISTA enhancers that show activity in the hindbrain overlap with Pet1 neuron TACs.
source: Of all experimentally validated VISTA enhancers that show activity in the hindbrain, 38% overlap with Pet1 neuron TACs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with the VISTA enhancer database.

claim: Only 1% of hindbrain-annotated VISTA enhancers overlap with Pet1 neuron-specific TACs.
source: However, only 1% of hindbrain-annotated VISTA enhancers overlap with Pet1 neuron-specific TACs, thus demonstrating that analyses of chromatin accessibility in low abundance neuron types can reveal previously unrecognized CREs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with the VISTA enhancer database and demonstrates the novelty of the findings.

claim: Genes associated with Pet1 neuron-specific TACs are enriched for axon and synapse functions.
source: Importantly, genes associated with Pet1 neuron-specific TACs are enriched for axon and synapse functions (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes linked to Pet1 neuron-specific TACs.

claim: Pet1 neuron-specific TACs were found for 5-HT neurotransmission genes.
source: Indeed, we found Pet1 neuron-specific TACs for 5-HT neurotransmission genes (Figure 1i–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and ChIPmentation data shown in Figure 1i-j.

claim: scATAC-seq using E14.5 flow sorted Pet1 neurons yielded >50,000 paired-end reads per nucleus.
source: The resulting scATAC-seq library was sequenced to a depth sufficient to yield >50,000 paired-end reads per nucleus.
evidence: The claim describes the sequencing depth achieved in the scATAC-seq experiment.

claim: After filtering, 1692 nuclei were retained for scATAC-seq analysis.
source: After filtering based on standard quality control measures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), we retained 1692 nuclei for analysis.
evidence: The claim describes the number of cells retained after quality control filtering.

claim: scATAC-seq identified 124,111 TACs, 60,117 of which were not identified in bulk Pet1 neuron ATAC-seq.
source: This led to the identification of 124,111 TACs, 60,117 of which were not identified in our bulk Pet1 neuron ATAC-seq (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of scATAC-seq and bulk ATAC-seq data.

claim: High concordance (Spearman's correlation = 0.9) was observed between pseudo-bulk scATAC-seq dataset and bulk ATAC-seq data.
source: We observed high concordance (Spearman's correlation = 0.9) between our pseudo-bulk scATAC-seq dataset and our bulk ATAC-seq data as illustrated by the highly similar TAC patterns in the Pet1 upstream enhancer region (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between scATAC-seq and bulk ATAC-seq data.

claim: scRNA-seq obtained over 80,000 reads per cell for 1612 cells, with a median of 4010 genes per cell and a total of 19,707 genes across all cells.
source: We obtained over 80,000 reads per cell for 1612 cells, with a median of 4010 genes per cell and a total of 19,707 genes across all cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: The claim describes the sequencing depth and gene detection in the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: 95% of the flow sorted Pet1 neurons robustly expressed both Pet1 and Yfp.
source: 95% of the flow sorted Pet1 neurons robustly expressed both Pet1 and Yfp, validating that our cell sorting method yields nearly pure samples of Pet1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing expression of Pet1 and Yfp in sorted cells.

claim: Single Pet1 neurons were grouped to identify 11 major subtypes with unique chromatin accessibility and expression patterns.
source: We grouped single Pet1 neurons to identify 11 major subtypes with unique chromatin accessibility and expression patterns (Figure 2d and f; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-d).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis of scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b loci TACs are robustly accessible in virtually all cells within the 11 identified subtypes.
source: Pet1 and Lmx1b loci TACs are robustly accessible in virtually all cells within the 11 identified subtypes (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by scATAC-seq data showing chromatin accessibility at Pet1 and Lmx1b loci.

claim: Two-thirds (63%) of TACs are broadly accessible among multiple subtypes.
source: Like Pet1 and Lmx1b, two-thirds (63%) of TACs are broadly accessible among multiple subtypes, including TACs of 5-HT neurotransmission genes Tph2, Slc22a3, and Slc6a4 (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TAC accessibility across scATAC-seq clusters.

claim: One-third of TACs (36.6%) are unique to a single cluster.
source: In contrast, one-third of TACs (36.6%) are unique to a single cluster.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TAC accessibility across scATAC-seq clusters.

claim: Six of the scATAC-seq clusters share a unique TAC region immediately upstream of the TSS of the rostral marker gene En1.
source: Six of the scATAC-seq clusters share a unique TAC region immediately upstream of the TSS of the rostral marker gene En1 while the remaining five clusters have more accessible TAC regions near the promoter of the caudal 5-HT neuron marker gene Meis2 (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by scATAC-seq data showing differential accessibility at En1 and Meis2 loci.

claim: 93% of the adult DRN cells map to the E14.5 Tph2/Slc6a4 and Pax5/En1 clusters that have high expression of rhombomere 1 markers.
source: Indeed, 93% of the adult DRN cells map to the E14.5 Tph2/Slc6a4 and Pax5/En1 clusters that have high expression of rhombomere 1 markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by UMAP projection of adult scRNA-seq data onto embryonic reference.

claim: Co-embedding scATAC-seq with scRNA-seq data yielded a total of 41,191 TAC-gene pairings.
source: Applying this method to our single-cell datasets yielded a total of 41,191 TAC-gene pairings (Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis linking TACs to genes using logistic regression.

claim: At E14.5, each gene is on average linked to only 1.8 TACs.
source: At this developmental time point, each gene is on average linked to only 1.8 TACs and most genes are associated with either none or a single TAC (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TAC-gene associations from integrated scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data.

claim: 10% of genes are associated with >5 TAC regions.
source: However, 10% of genes are associated with >5 TAC regions, and a select group of genes (0.045%) are associated with >20 TACs (Figure 2h–j; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TAC-gene associations showing a subset of genes with many linked regulatory elements.

claim: The top 1500 genes with the highest number of linked CREs are highly enriched for genes involved in axon and synapse development.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the top 1500 genes with the highest number of linked CREs revealed that they are highly enriched for genes involved in axon and synapse development (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes with many linked TACs.

claim: The expression of 5-HT identity genes Tph2, Slc6a4, and Slc22a3 are low or undetectable in most Pet1 neurons at E14.5 despite their relatively uniform accessible chromatin.
source: However, we noticed that the expression of 5-HT identity genes Tph2, Slc6a4, and Slc22a3 are low or undetectable in most Pet1 neurons at E14.5 despite their relatively uniform accessible chromatin in Pet1 neurons at this stage (Figure 2e and g).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data showing accessible chromatin without corresponding gene expression.

claim: The vast majority of Pet1-lineage neurons robustly express 5-HT identity genes in the adult mouse brain.
source: The vast majority of Pet1-lineage neurons robustly express these 5-HT identity genes in the adult mouse brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e; Donovan et al., 2019; Okaty et al., 2015; Okaty et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and citations to published studies.

claim: Developmental state accounted for the majority of variance in PCA of Pet1 neuron ATAC-seq at E11.5, E14.5, and E17.5.
source: PCA showed high concordance of ATAC-seq replicates within each time point with developmental state accounting for the majority of variance (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of ATAC-seq data across developmental time points.

claim: 16,493 TACs open (gain accessibility) between E11.5 and E14.5.
source: Of the TACs detected in Pet1 neurons, 16,493 open, that is, gain accessibility (fold change >2 and FDR < 0.01) between E11.5 and E14.5, while 4148 open from E14.5 to E17.5 (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential accessibility analysis of ATAC-seq data across developmental stages.

claim: 9,402 E11.5 TACs close (lose accessibility) by E14.5.
source: Concurrently, 9,402 E11.5 TACs close, that is, lose accessibility (fold change >2 and FDR < 0.01) by E14.5, and 1504 TACs close between E14.5 and E17.5 (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential accessibility analysis of ATAC-seq data across developmental stages.

claim: Active enhancers are over-represented among TACs opening between E11.5 and E17.5.
source: Assessment of chromatin states showed that active enhancers are over-represented among TACs opening between E11.5 and E17.5 (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1e-g).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChromHMM analysis of histone modifications at dynamic TACs.

claim: 93% of Pet1 neuron super-enhancer TACs either gain or lose accessibility between E11.5 and E17.5.
source: Pet1 neuron super-enhancer accessibility is particularly highly dynamic during postmitotic neuron maturation, with the vast majority (93%) of TACs either gaining or losing accessibility between E11.5 and E17.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of super-enhancer accessibility dynamics across developmental stages.

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility at cis-regulatory regions are significantly correlated with the temporal expression trajectories of their target genes.
source: Using our TAC-to-gene assignments derived from single-cell data (Figure 2i–j), we found that changes in chromatin accessibility at cis-regulatory regions are significantly correlated with the temporal expression trajectories of their target genes (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data showing correlation between accessibility and expression changes.

claim: Genes associated with closing TACs are important for neural precursor functions.
source: GO analysis revealed that genes associated with closing TACs are important for neural precursor functions, whereas the genes linked to opening TACs are strongly enriched for axon development between E11.5 and E14.5 and synaptic signaling between E14.5 and E17.5 (Figure 3g–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes linked to dynamic TACs.

claim: Genes linked to opening TACs are strongly enriched for axon development between E11.5 and E14.5 and synaptic signaling between E14.5 and E17.5.
source: GO analysis revealed that genes associated with closing TACs are important for neural precursor functions, whereas the genes linked to opening TACs are strongly enriched for axon development between E11.5 and E14.5 and synaptic signaling between E14.5 and E17.5 (Figure 3g–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes linked to dynamic TACs.

claim: TACs that are unique to Pet1-lineage neurons are enriched for ETS-factor binding sites.
source: Notably, TACs that are unique to Pet1-lineage neurons are enriched for ETS-factor binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of Pet1 neuron-specific TACs.

claim: Pet1-deficient Pet1-lineage neurons cluster closely with wildtype Pet1 neurons in PCA.
source: PCA of ATAC-seq datasets obtained from Pet1-EYFP-positive, Pet1-/- hindbrain cells at E11.5, E14.5, and E17.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b-c) showed that Pet1-deficient Pet1-lineage neurons (Pet1-/- neurons) cluster closely with wildtype Pet1 neurons (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of ATAC-seq data from wildtype and Pet1-/- neurons.

claim: There is a striking overall reduction of Pet1 footprints and decreased accessibility of many TSS-distal TACs in Pet1-/- neurons compared to wildtype neurons at all three embryonic stages.
source: However, we found a striking overall reduction of Pet1 footprints and decreased accessibility of many TSS-distal TACs in Pet1-/- neurons compared to wildtype neurons at all three embryonic stages (Figure 4b–c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by footprinting analysis and differential accessibility analysis of ATAC-seq data from Pet1-/- neurons.

claim: Pet1 directly occupies at least 53% of Pet1-dependent TACs.
source: CUT&RUN data showed that Pet1 directly occupies at least 53% of Pet1-dependent TACs (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by CUT&RUN data showing Pet1 occupancy at differentially accessible regions.

claim: 73% of all Pet1-regulated TACs are TACs unique to Pet1 neurons.
source: Moreover, 73% of all Pet1-regulated TACs and 80% of Pet1-regulated TACs with Pet1 occupancy are TACs unique to Pet1 neurons (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Pet1-regulated TACs and their cell-type specificity.

claim: 80% of Pet1-regulated TACs with Pet1 occupancy are TACs unique to Pet1 neurons.
source: Moreover, 73% of all Pet1-regulated TACs and 80% of Pet1-regulated TACs with Pet1 occupancy are TACs unique to Pet1 neurons (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Pet1-regulated TACs with Pet1 occupancy and their cell-type specificity.

claim: Pet1-dependent TACs with direct Pet1 occupancy show strong enrichment for serotonin biosynthesis genes.
source: Highest FDR GO terms for Pet1-dependent TACs (in red) that are occupied by Pet1 show strong enrichment for serotonin biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes linked to Pet1-occupied, Pet1-dependent TACs shown in Figure 4g.

claim: There is a significant loss of accessibility of enhancers either upstream of the TSS or within introns of Tph2, Gch1, and Ddc in Pet1-/- neurons.
source: Indeed, we found a significant loss of accessibility of enhancers either upstream of the TSS or within introns of Tph2, Gch1, and Ddc (Figure 4i).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing reduced accessibility at 5-HT synthesis gene enhancers in Pet1-/- neurons.

claim: TACs associated with the serotonin reuptake transporter genes Slc22a3 and Slc6a4 are significantly reduced in accessibility in Pet1-/- neurons.
source: TACs associated with the serotonin reuptake transporter genes Slc22a3 and Slc6a4 are also significantly reduced in accessibility (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing reduced accessibility at serotonin transporter gene enhancers in Pet1-/- neurons.

claim: TACs that require Pet1 for accessibility are mostly unique to Pet1 neurons.
source: Importantly, TACs that require Pet1 for accessibility are mostly unique to Pet1 neurons, while TACs of 5-HT pathway genes that are not Pet1 neuron-specific are not significantly affected by Pet1 deficiency (Figure 4i–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Pet1-dependent TACs and their cell-type specificity.

claim: Enhancers associated with Slc6a4 that are directly occupied by Pet1 show little accessibility at E11.5 but gradually gain accessibility from E11.5 to E17.5 in wildtype Pet1 neurons.
source: Interestingly, the enhancers associated with Slc6a4 that are directly occupied by Pet1 show little accessibility to transposase at E11.5 but gradually gain accessibility from E11.5 to E17.5 in wildtype Pet1 neurons (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing temporal dynamics of Slc6a4 enhancer accessibility.

claim: Slc6a4 enhancer regions fail to fully open in Pet1-/- neurons.
source: In contrast, these TAC regions fail to fully open in Pet1-/- neurons (Figure 4j), suggesting Pet1 is directly required for initial conversion of these regions to a euchromatic state.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data comparing Slc6a4 enhancer accessibility in wildtype and Pet1-/- neurons.

claim: 47 TAC regions fail to fully open between E11.5 and E17.5 in Pet1-/- neurons, 20 of which show direct Pet1 occupancy at E14.5.
source: Among the Pet1-regulated TACs, we identified 47 regions that similarly fail to fully open between E11.5 and E17.5 in Pet1-/- neurons, 20 of which show direct Pet1 occupancy at E14.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TACs that require Pet1 for chromatin opening and Pet1 CUT&RUN data.

claim: TACs that require Pet1 for chromatin opening are linked to genes enriched for synaptic products.
source: TACs that require Pet1 for chromatin opening are linked to genes enriched for synaptic products, suggesting that Pet1 opens condensed chromatin at TACs controlling synapse functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes linked to TACs requiring Pet1 for opening.

claim: 1834 Pet1-maintained TACs that are mainly distal CREs in wildtype Pet1 neurons lose their accessibility in Pet1-cKO.
source: We found 1834 Pet1-maintained TACs that are mainly distal CREs in wildtype Pet1 neurons lose their accessibility in Pet1-cKO (Figure 5a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential accessibility analysis of ATAC-seq data from Pet1-cKO neurons.

claim: 936 Pet1-maintained TACs do not change in wildtype neurons from E11.5 to E14.5, indicating that Pet1 is required to sustain TACs after they open.
source: The accessibility of 936 of these TACs does not change in wildtype neurons from E11.5 to E14.5, indicating that Pet1 is required to sustain TACs after they open (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TACs that are stable in wildtype but lost in Pet1-cKO, indicating a maintenance function for Pet1.

claim: Many 5-HT neurotransmission gene TACs lose accessibility in Pet1-cKO including the enhancers of Tph2, Gch1, Ddc, and Slc22a3.
source: Many 5-HT neurotransmission gene TACs lose accessibility as in Pet1-/- neurons including the enhancers of 5-HT neurotransmission genes Tph2, Gch1, Ddc, and Slc22a3 (Figure 5f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing reduced accessibility at 5-HT neurotransmission gene enhancers in Pet1-cKO neurons.

claim: Pet1 directly occupies the TAC that overlaps with its autoregulatory enhancer.
source: CUT&RUN showed that Pet1 directly occupies the TAC that overlaps with its autoregulatory enhancer (Scott et al., 2005a; Scott et al., 2005b), which is consistent with our previous Pet1 ChIP-seq findings (Wyler et al., 2016; Figure 5h; Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by CUT&RUN data and is consistent with previous ChIP-seq data.

claim: Pet1 is required for optimal accessibility of its autoregulatory enhancer region and for sustaining its accessibility.
source: We found that Pet1 is required for optimal accessibility of this enhancer region and for sustaining its accessibility suggesting that maintenance of chromatin accessibility at autoregulatory enhancers is an important mechanism for terminal selector autoregulation (Figure 5h).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing reduced accessibility at the Pet1 autoregulatory enhancer in Pet1-cKO neurons.

claim: A significant portion of Pet1 and Lmx1b binding sites coincide within the same TAC regions.
source: Lmx1b CUT&RUN in E14.5 Pet1 neurons, which revealed that a significant portion of Pet1 and Lmx1b binding sites coincide within the same TAC regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: The claim is supported by CUT&RUN data showing co-occupancy of Pet1 and Lmx1b.

claim: In Lmx1b-cKO Pet1 neurons, chromatin landscape is altered.
source: In Lmx1b-cKO (Lmx1bfl/fl; Pet1-Cre;Rosa26Ai9) Pet1 neurons (Donovan et al., 2019; Figure 6—figure supplement 1d-f), chromatin landscape is altered (Figure 6a)
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of ATAC-seq data from Lmx1b-cKO neurons.

claim: More TACs are differentially accessible in Lmx1b-cKO neurons than in Pet1-cKO neurons.
source: and more TACs are differentially accessible than in Pet1-cKO neurons (Figures 5a and 6c), suggesting that Lmx1b has a broader impact than Pet1 on 5-HT neuron chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of differential accessibility analysis between Lmx1b-cKO and Pet1-cKO neurons.

claim: Lmx1b directly binds 19% of the differentially accessible TACs in Lmx1b-cKO.
source: Lmx1b directly binds 19% of the differentially accessible TACs in Lmx1b-cKO (comparable to Pet1 which binds 20% of differentially accessible TACs in Pet1-cKO) indicating direct maintenance of accessibility by Lmx1b at those regions (Figure 6d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1m)
evidence: The claim is supported by CUT&RUN data showing Lmx1b occupancy at differentially accessible regions in Lmx1b-cKO.

claim: Lmx1b-dependent TACs with direct Lmx1b occupancy are most significantly associated with monoamine/serotonin synthesis.
source: The Lmx1b-dependent TACs with direct Lmx1b occupancy, of which 65% are specific to Pet1 neurons (Figure 6i), are also most significantly associated with monoamine/serotonin synthesis (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes linked to Lmx1b-occupied, Lmx1b-dependent TACs.

claim: The conditional ablation of Lmx1b results in an even greater closing of 5-HT neurotransmission gene TACs than Pet1 ablation.
source: Moreover, the conditional ablation of Lmx1b results in an even greater closing of 5-HT neurotransmission gene TACs than Pet1 ablation (Figure 6j–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq data from Lmx1b-cKO and Pet1-cKO neurons showing greater accessibility loss in Lmx1b-cKO.

claim: Many TACs whose accessibility was not significantly reduced in Pet1-cKO neurons significantly lost accessibility in Lmx1b-cKO neurons.
source: Many TACs whose accessibility was not significantly reduced in Pet1-cKO neurons (fold change >2, FDR < 0.01) significantly lost accessibility in Lmx1b-cKO neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1j) including the TACs of Gchfr, Slc18a2, and Maoa (Figure 6j–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of differential accessibility between Pet1-cKO and Lmx1b-cKO neurons.

claim: Lmx1b directly occupies the enhancers of many 5-HT neurotransmission genes whose expression is critically dependent on Lmx1b.
source: Lmx1b directly occupies the enhancers of many 5-HT neurotransmission genes (Figure 6j–k) whose expression is known to be critically dependent on Lmx1b (Ding et al., 2003; Donovan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by CUT&RUN data showing Lmx1b occupancy and citations to studies showing Lmx1b-dependent gene expression.

claim: The loss of chromatin accessibility in Lmx1b-cKO is highly similar to that in Pet1 and Lmx1b double conditional knockout (DKO) Pet1 neurons.
source: We also found that the loss of chromatin accessibility in Lmx1b-cKO is highly similar to that in Pet1 and Lmx1b double conditional knockout (DKO: Lmx1bfl/fl; Pet1fl/fl; Pet1-Cre; Rosa26Ai9) Pet1 neurons (Figure 6b–c , and g–h)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of differential accessibility analysis between Lmx1b-cKO and DKO neurons.

claim: The ablation of both Pet1 and Lmx1b does not have greater effect than ablation of Lmx1b alone.
source: suggesting that the ablation of both TFs does not have greater effect than ablation of Lmx1b alone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of chromatin accessibility changes in Lmx1b-cKO and DKO neurons.

claim: At a substantial subset of Lmx1b-dependent TACs such as those of Tph2, Gch1, Ddc, and Slc6a4, Pet1 and Lmx1b non-redundantly co-regulate the accessibility of the CREs.
source: At a substantial subset of Lmx1b-dependent TACs such as those of Tph2, Gch1, Ddc, and Slc6a4 (Figures 5f–g ,–6j–k), Pet1 and Lmx1b non-redundantly co-regulate the accessibility of the CREs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing that both Pet1 and Lmx1b are required for full accessibility at certain enhancers.

claim: Lmx1b sustains, independent of Pet1, an additional subset of TACs that are required for axon and synaptic formation, neurotrophin signaling, and neuronal growth.
source: In parallel, Lmx1b further sustains, independent of Pet1, an additional subset of TACs that are required for axon and synaptic formation, neurotrophin signaling, and neuronal growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1i-j).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of TACs that are Lmx1b-dependent but not Pet1-dependent.

claim: The binding sites of several TF families such as the Rfx-related factors are less accessible in Pet1- and Lmx1b-deficient Pet1 neurons.
source: Motif analysis on the differentially accessible regions in the cKO and DKO neurons showed that the binding sites of several TF families such as the Rfx-related factors are less accessible in Pet1- and Lmx1b-deficient Pet1 neurons, demonstrating that together Pet1 and Lmx1b shape the global gene regulatory landscape of available TF binding sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of differentially accessible regions in cKO and DKO neurons.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b program TAC accessibility of many genes involved in axon growth and synaptic functions.
source: In addition to controlling TACs associated with 5-HT transmission genes that define serotonergic identity (Figure 6h), Pet1 and Lmx1b program TAC accessibility of many genes involved in axon growth and synaptic functions (Figure 7a; Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of Pet1- and Lmx1b-regulated TACs.

claim: The majority of regulated TACs identified from Lmx1b-cKO and DKO neurons are those that gain accessibility in wildtype Pet1 neurons from E11.5 to E17.5.
source: The majority of regulated TACs identified from Lmx1b-cKO and DKO neurons are those that gain accessibility in wildtype Pet1 neurons from E11.5 to E17.5 (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the temporal dynamics of Pet1- and Lmx1b-regulated TACs.

claim: The Pet1- and Lmx1b-dependent TACs of Syt1 and Slc17a8 are Pet1 neuron specific.
source: The Pet1- and Lmx1b-dependent TACs of Syt1 and Slc17a8 are Pet1 neuron specific, suggesting that the expression of some widely expressed neuronal genes are regulated in different neurons by neuron-type-specific CREs (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing that Syt1 and Slc17a8 TACs are specific to Pet1 neurons.

claim: Syt1 and Slc17a8 expression are decreased in Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO neurons.
source: In support of the contribution of these Pet1- and Lmx1b-regulated enhancers to developmental gene expression, Syt1 and Slc17a8 expression are decreased in Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO neurons (Figure 7d).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing reduced expression of Syt1 and Slc17a8 in cKO and DKO neurons.

claim: There is significant correlation between TACs that close in Lmx1b-cKO and DKO and the expression of the linked genes.
source: Further, there is significant correlation between TACs that close in Lmx1b-cKO and DKO and the expression of the linked genes (Figure 7e).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between chromatin accessibility changes and gene expression changes.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b collectively maintain the transcriptome necessary for axon, synapse, and dendrite development.
source: GO analysis of down-regulated genes in DKO neurons revealed that Pet1 and Lmx1b collectively maintain the transcriptome necessary for axon, synapse, and dendrite development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of down-regulated genes in DKO neurons.

claim: 5-HT pericellular baskets were readily identified in wildtype brains by postnatal day 15 (P15).
source: We found that by postnatal day 15 (P15), 5-HT pericellular baskets were readily identified in wildtype brains.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing pericellular baskets in wildtype mice.

claim: Some 5-HT axons reach the dLS in Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO mice.
source: Further, as expected, some 5-HT axons reach the dLS in Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO mice (Figure 7f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing TdTomato-positive axons in the dLS of cKO and DKO mice.

claim: Pericellular baskets could not be found in the remaining 5-HT axons in Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO mice.
source: However, pericellular baskets could not be found in the remaining 5-HT axons (Figure 7f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing absence of pericellular baskets in cKO and DKO mice.

claim: Co-localization of Syt1 and vGlut3 immunostaining with TdTomato-positive axon terminals is significantly reduced in Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO mice compared to wildtype animals.
source: Of the few axonal terminals that do reach postsynaptic cell bodies, co-localization of Syt1 and vGlut3 immunostaining with TdTomato-positive axon terminals is significantly reduced compared to wildtype animals (Figure 7h–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and quantification showing reduced co-localization in cKO and DKO mice.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b control accessibility of putative CREs for genes that are required for 5-HT axon extension and formation of presynaptic structure that enables 5-HT and glutamatergic co-transmission.
source: This suggests that Pet1 and Lmx1b control accessibility of putative CREs for genes that are required for 5-HT axon extension and formation of presynaptic structure that enables 5-HT and glutamatergic co-transmission.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, and immunohistochemistry data showing that Pet1 and Lmx1b regulate chromatin accessibility and expression of synapse genes, and that loss of these factors impairs synapse formation.

claim: Distal enhancers define the Pet1 neuron lineage that generates serotonin (5-HT) neurons in mice.
source: Here, we show that unique distal enhancers define the Pet1 neuron lineage that generates serotonin (5-HT) neurons in mice.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the ATAC-seq and ChIPmentation data showing Pet1 neuron-specific distal enhancers.

claim: Heterogeneous single-cell chromatin landscapes are established early in postmitotic Pet1 neurons.
source: Heterogeneous single-cell chromatin landscapes are established early in postmitotic Pet1 neurons and reveal the putative regulatory programs driving Pet1 neuron subtype identities.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the scATAC-seq data showing 11 distinct Pet1 neuron subtypes at E14.5.

claim: Distal enhancer accessibility is highly dynamic as Pet1 neurons mature.
source: Distal enhancer accessibility is highly dynamic as Pet1 neurons mature, suggesting the existence of regulatory factors that reorganize postmitotic neuronal chromatin.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the temporal ATAC-seq data showing dynamic changes in TAC accessibility from E11.5 to E17.5.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b control chromatin accessibility to select Pet1-lineage-specific enhancers for 5-HT neurotransmission.
source: We find that Pet1 and Lmx1b control chromatin accessibility to select Pet1-lineage-specific enhancers for 5-HT neurotransmission.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the ATAC-seq data from Pet1-cKO, Lmx1b-cKO, and DKO neurons showing reduced accessibility at 5-HT neurotransmission gene enhancers.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b are required to maintain chromatin accessibility during early maturation.
source: Additionally, these factors are required to maintain chromatin accessibility during early maturation suggesting that postmitotic neuronal open chromatin is unstable and requires continuous regulatory input.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the ATAC-seq data from Pet1-cKO neurons showing that TACs that are stable in wildtype lose accessibility when Pet1 is conditionally deleted.

claim: Postmitotic neuronal open chromatin is unstable and requires continuous regulatory input.
source: Additionally, these factors are required to maintain chromatin accessibility during early maturation suggesting that postmitotic neuronal open chromatin is unstable and requires continuous regulatory input.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that chromatin accessibility is lost when Pet1 or Lmx1b are conditionally deleted, suggesting ongoing requirement for these factors.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b are terminal selector TFs in 5-HT neurons.
source: The ETS domain factor Pet1 and the LIM homeodomain (HD) factor Lmx1b are terminal selector TFs in 5-HT neurons as they are continuously expressed beginning at the postmitotic precursor stage, control their own expression through direct positive autoregulation, and are required for the acquisition of 5-HT neuron terminal identity through sequence-specific transcriptional activation of 5-HT pathway genes (Deneris and Gaspar, 2018; Hobert, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published reviews summarizing the known functions of Pet1 and Lmx1b.

claim: Pet1 and Lmx1b are required for the acquisition of serotonergic firing characteristics and formation of long-distance profusely arborized 5-HT axon architectures.
source: Pet1 and Lmx1b are also required for the acquisition of serotonergic firing characteristics and formation of long-distance profusely arborized 5-HT axon architectures throughout the brain and spinal cord (Donovan et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2010; Wyler et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies showing the requirement for Pet1 and Lmx1b in 5-HT neuron development.

claim: Biallelic loss of function of FEV, the human ortholog of Pet1, has been identified in autism cases.
source: Pet1's function in 5-HT neurons is clinically significant as recent studies identified biallelic loss of function of FEV, the human ortholog of Pet1, in autism cases suggesting that defects in transcriptional control of 5-HT neurons are a potential path to human neurodevelopmental disorders (Doan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study identifying FEV mutations in autism.
